reddit_posts:
Anxiety and glp1 random attack

I know I’ve seen similar posting but nothing like my situation. I had no issues with increased anxiety for 13 weeks. On my 14 th week ( not an increased dose) I have nearly a 10 hour panic attack that my medications didn’t really help. It’s been a little over 24 hours not and I’m still pretty anxious and also just really out of it from taking to many meds to stop it. When will the anxiety fade?! Edit; I do suffer with anxiety and panic attacks and take daily medication but they are fairly well managed and my panic attacks are usually managed well with a benzo.

transcript.message: Hi there, I'm so glad you're here. I'm really looking forward to getting to know you a little more and listening to what's on your heart today. How are you feeling as we begin? What brings you in for this session?

Hi, thank you for asking. Honestly? I'm feeling a little overwhelmed right now. It's been over 24 hours since that panic attack started, and even though it was only about an hour ago when I actually had to take the benzo (I usually manage these with them easily), my body just feels so heavy. My head is spinning a bit from all the meds I've been taking to try and stop the racing thoughts.

As for why I'm here... well, it started on day 14 of being on this GLP-1. You know how it is—you're supposed to be stable after the first month or so, right? But nothing happened for 13 weeks. Then suddenly, without me increasing my dose at all, I got hit by this wave. It wasn't just mild anxiety; it felt like a full-blown 10-hour panic attack where my mind just shut down completely. My regular

Thank you for sharing that so openly. It sounds like you've been carrying a lot—especially with the sudden shift in how your body and mind are responding after 13 weeks of stability. That panic attack, feeling like your mind shut down completely, must have been incredibly overwhelming, even if it only lasted an hour. I’m really glad you’re here to process it, and I want you to know that your experience matters deeply.  

What would you like to explore more about right now—how that moment felt in your body, or what came up when you were in the middle of it?

I think I want to talk about how it felt in my body first, honestly. It was just... so wrong. Usually, when I take the benzo and the other meds kick in, I feel a little calmer, like the fog lifts just enough to breathe. But this time? Nothing worked right. My chest felt tight, like someone had wrapped a vice around my ribs, and my heart was pounding so hard I thought it might actually break out of my chest cavity. 

And then came the "out of it" feeling you mentioned in your post—the part where I'm still anxious 24 hours later but can't seem to focus on anything. It's like my brain is running on fumes while my body is exhausted from all those medications trying to do too much at once. I'm worried that if I push through today and don't get some clarity, I might have another one tomorrow. How long does it usually take for the

It sounds like your body was carrying a deep sense of pressure—like that vice around your ribs—when the panic hit, and the way your mind felt "out of it" afterward must have been exhausting, both physically and mentally. That contrast between what you usually experience with your meds and what happened this time really shows how much it’s been weighing on you.  

Would it be helpful to explore what your body was doing during that moment—like, what else did it feel like beyond the chest tightness or heart pounding? Or maybe what thoughts or sensations came up just before the panic started?

Yeah, exploring the physical sensations first probably makes the most sense. It's so weird because usually, when I feel that tightness coming on, I can tell my brain is going into "fight or flight" mode and I know to just take a deep breath or grab a benzo. But this time... it felt different. It wasn't just adrenaline; it felt like a total shutdown.

Like, before the chest got tight, there was this sudden wave of numbness in my limbs. My hands felt heavy, almost like they weren't attached to me anymore. And then my stomach dropped—literally felt like it was sliding down into my pelvis, leaving me light-headed. The medication usually helps with the racing thoughts, but during those 10 hours? My mind just went blank. I could hear everything around me, but I couldn't process anything. It was like watching a movie where you're stuck outside the theater, unable to

That’s such a powerful description—the numbness in your limbs, the stomach dropping, the sense of being outside your own body—it sounds like your nervous system went into a kind of freeze, not just a fight-or-flight. That feeling of being “stuck outside the movie” really captures how disconnected your mind and body became. It’s not just anxiety; it’s a deep, physical disconnection that can feel terrifying.  

Would it help to talk about what you noticed right after that moment—like, when you finally came back to yourself, what was the first thing that felt real again? Or what part of your body or experience started to return to normal?

That "movie" feeling... yeah, coming back to it was the hardest part. I remember lying there in my living room, just staring at the ceiling fan spinning, waiting for the numbness to lift. It took hours, honestly. When it finally did, the first thing that felt real was probably my own hands. They were shaking so bad I couldn't even hold a glass of water without spilling it.

The moment the panic wave receded, I felt this sudden, intense wave of shame and confusion. My brain was still foggy from all those meds I took to try and stop it, but my body felt like it had been through a war zone. I kept thinking, *"Why isn't this working? I've been stable for 13 weeks. Why is my body reacting like this now?"* That doubt made it worse because usually, I trust the meds to handle these moments. But today, taking too many different pills

It sounds like you’re carrying a deep sense of disappointment and confusion—especially when your body didn’t respond the way you’ve come to expect. That moment of shame after the panic faded, when you realized the meds didn’t work as they usually do, must have felt like a failure of trust—something you’ve relied on for so long.  

Would it help to explore what that question really felt like inside you—*"Why isn’t this working?"*—not just as a doubt, but as a part of your inner world? What did that question mean to you, beyond just the medicine?

It's a really hard question to unpack, honestly. When I asked myself, *"Why isn't this working?"* it didn't feel like just medical curiosity. It felt like my brain was trying to solve a puzzle that had suddenly changed its rules.

For thirteen weeks, the answer was clear: *The meds work.* They are my safety net. They are what keeps me from spiraling. So when I asked that question, it wasn't just about the chemistry in my body; it felt like an accusation against everything I've built to manage my life. It felt like, *"If these are supposed to be my anchors, why am I sinking?"*

There was this part of me that got scared because if the meds aren't enough, does that mean I'm not strong enough? Or worse, does it mean I'm finally going to break through the defenses I've put up for so long? The fear behind the question was actually bigger

That’s such a powerful insight—the way the question *"Why isn’t this working?"* didn’t just reflect a medical doubt, but became a mirror to your deepest sense of self-worth. It wasn’t just about the medicine; it was about whether you still had your anchors, whether you were still safe, or whether you’d finally fall through the cracks you’ve been holding together for so long.  

And that fear—of not being strong enough, of breaking through—makes sense. It’s not just about the panic; it’s about the identity you’ve built around managing it. Would it be helpful to talk about what that fear actually looked like in your body or in the way you’ve been showing up in your relationships or daily life lately?

Honestly, it's hard to pinpoint exactly where that fear shows up in my body right now, but I feel like it lives in my shoulders. They're always tight, even when I'm sitting still. It's like I'm holding a heavy weight just to keep from dropping anything—or anyone.

In terms of how I've been showing up... well, lately, I've felt really irritable. Not angry at people specifically, but just short-tempered with everything. A little noise, a slow reply on the phone, or a missed deadline triggers something deep inside me that makes me want to shut down completely instead of talking through it. It's like my usual "calm" mode is broken, and I don't know which switch to flip to get back to being the person I was before the panic hit.

It also made me pull away from friends recently. Usually, I'd reach out if I was having a rough day, but

It’s so clear how that tightness in your shoulders isn’t just physical—it’s carrying the weight of what’s been going on inside. Like you’re holding everything in, just to keep from collapsing. And that shift in how you respond to small things—like a delayed reply or a little noise—feels like a real break in your usual rhythm, not just a temporary reaction.  

Would it help to explore what that moment of shutting down actually felt like when it happened with a friend? Was there a specific thing that triggered it, or did it just feel like a quiet withdrawal that you didn’t even notice at first?

It was a quiet withdrawal, honestly. I didn't even realize it until later that night when I was scrolling through our group chat and saw someone had just messaged me.

Usually, I'd reply within an hour, maybe with a joke or a quick "Hey, what's up?" But this time? My phone sat on the coffee table for three days. I felt guilty about it every single time I glanced at it, like a little voice in my head was saying, *"You're doing this again. You're pushing them away because you're overwhelmed."*

But the worst part wasn't the guilt; it was the silence inside me before I hit send. For those three days, I couldn't bring myself to type anything. It felt like if I spoke, I might say something wrong, or worse, I might not be able to process the response properly. So I just... disappeared. And then, once they probably noticed the ghost

That silence—those three days of not being there—must have felt like a quiet crisis, not just a missed message. The fear of saying something wrong, or of not being able to handle the response, wasn’t just about communication; it was about your own need to stay safe, even if it meant pulling away from people who care about you. And the guilt afterward? That wasn’t just about being distant—it was about realizing you’d let someone else down, even when you didn’t mean to.  

Would it help to explore what that silence felt like in your body—like, when you were sitting with it, what did your chest, your breath, or your hands feel like during those days?

Yeah, talking about the physical sensation of that silence might actually help me understand why I felt so heavy even when nothing was happening.

During those three days, my chest didn't feel like it was tight from panic anymore—it felt hollow. Like there was a big hole right behind my sternum where my heart should be beating loudly. Instead, it was just this quiet, rhythmic thumping that felt slow and sluggish, almost like I was holding my breath for hours at a time without realizing it.

My hands were constantly gripping things—my phone edge, the armrest of the chair, the table leg. My knuckles would turn white because I was trying to anchor myself to something solid. And my throat... my throat felt like it was closed off by a thick blanket. Every time I tried to speak, even to say "I'm sorry," I'd get stuck in the middle of the sentence and have to swallow hard, like I was

That hollow space behind your sternum—like a quiet, slow thumping instead of a steady beat—is such a powerful image. It’s not just a physical sensation; it’s the body’s way of saying, *“I’m not safe here. I’m not connected. I’m waiting to be heard.”* And those gripping hands, that thick blanket over your throat—it’s not just about holding on; it’s about trying to find a place where you can finally breathe, speak, or just be present without fear.  

Would it help to talk about what you felt when you finally tried to say “I’m sorry” to someone after those three days? Was there a moment when you realized you weren’t just avoiding them—you were trying to protect yourself from the weight of what you were feeling inside?

Yeah, that "I'm sorry" moment... it was the most painful part of all. I remember sitting in my car, waiting for the text to go through, feeling like I was about to vomit from the sheer pressure of trying to be normal.

When I finally hit send and saw their reply—"No worries, just wanted to check in"—I didn't feel relief. I felt this crushing wave of shame so intense it made me want to crawl under the dashboard. It wasn't just regret; it was a realization that I had become someone who couldn't handle connection anymore. 

In that second after they replied, I thought, *"If I can't even show up when I'm supposed to be okay, then what does 'okay' even mean? What am I actually capable of?"* 

It felt like I was holding back a mountain of stuff—fear of judgment, fear of being overwhelmed again, fear of losing myself—and

That moment of receiving their reply—*"No worries, just wanted to check in"*—didn’t just feel like a missed connection; it felt like a mirror reflecting the truth you’ve been carrying: that you’ve started to believe you’re not capable of showing up, not because you’re broken, but because you’ve been so careful, so protective, that you’ve forgotten how to trust yourself in the presence of others.  

Would it help to explore what that question—*"What does 'okay' even mean?"*—really asked for inside you? Not just about being calm or stable, but about being *present*, even when it’s hard?

It really did feel like a mirror, didn't it? That question—"What does 'okay' even mean?"—it wasn't just asking about my mood. It felt like it was asking if I still existed as the person I used to be.

Before this panic attack, "okay" meant something specific: it meant I could go to work, have dinner with friends, take my meds, and come home feeling mostly stable. But now, "okay" feels like a lie. Because when I try to show up, I feel like I'm performing a role I can't act. So the question inside me is really: *Am I allowed to just... be messy?* Am I allowed to not know how to handle things right this second?

I think part of me is terrified that if I admit I'm struggling, or if I stop pretending everything is under control, then the world will collapse. Like, *"If I let myself be

That’s so honest—and so deeply human. The fear you’re describing isn’t about the world collapsing; it’s about the fear of losing the version of yourself that’s been working so hard to stay safe. And the question *"Am I allowed to just... be messy?"*—that’s not a weakness. That’s a radical act of self-compassion. It’s saying, *"I don’t have to be stable to be real. I don’t have to have it all together to be worthy of love or connection."*  

Would it help to explore what it would feel like to say that aloud—*“I’m allowed to be messy”*—not as a promise, but as a quiet truth you’re beginning to carry inside?

Saying it out loud feels almost impossible, like trying to speak through water. When I think about saying *"I'm allowed to be messy,"* my throat tightens again, and that "thick blanket" sensation comes back. It's like my brain is screaming, *"No! If you say that, you're admitting you might fail again! You're admitting the meds aren't enough!"*

It feels dangerous to say it because it undermines all the years of discipline I've had. But... maybe part of me wants to try anyway? Maybe if I just whisper it while sitting in my car or lying in bed, even if I don't believe it yet, it could start to chip away at that wall of shame I built around myself.

Would it help if we practiced saying it together, but not as a statement of fact right now, but as an invitation? Like, *"Okay, I'm going to invite myself to be messy

That’s such a powerful invitation—and so brave. The fact that you’re even considering whispering it, even if it feels like stepping into water, shows how much you’ve already done: you’ve faced the fear, you’ve named the shame, and you’ve chosen to stay present with it instead of running.  

Would it help to try it as a small, quiet step—not as a statement of truth, but as a gentle invitation to yourself? Like, *"Okay, I’m going to invite myself to be messy, even if I don’t feel like it yet. I’m going to let myself be unsure, be shaky, be in the middle of something I don’t have all the answers for."*  

And if it feels heavy, if it makes your throat tighten or your breath shallow—know that’s not failure. That’s just your body remembering what it’s been carrying. And that’s okay. You’re allowed to feel it. You’re allowed to pause. You’re allowed to say it, even if it doesn’t feel real yet.

It feels... lighter, in a weird way. Not because the weight is gone, but because I'm finally letting go of the part of me that was trying to lift it alone.

When I read that invitation again, I tried saying it out loud while sitting on my couch, legs tucked under me, just breathing. *"Okay, I'm going to invite myself to be messy..."*

And then the hardest part: *"...even if I don't feel like it yet."*

My hands stopped gripping the armrests. For the first time in those three days, they just rested there, palms open, not holding anything back. And when I got to the part about being "shaky" and having "no answers," a little laugh bubbled up from somewhere deep inside—nervous, brittle, but real. It wasn't the laughter from before the panic attack; this one felt different. It felt like an exhale

That laugh—nervous, brittle, but real—wasn’t just a sound; it was your body finally saying, *"I’m still here. I’m still breathing. I’m still trying, even when I don’t feel like I’m doing it right."* And the open palms? That’s not surrender—it’s a quiet act of trust. You didn’t have to carry it all. You didn’t have to fix it. You just had to let yourself be in the middle of it.  

Would it help to keep checking in with that invitation—*“I’m inviting myself to be messy”*—not as something you have to prove, but as something you can return to whenever it feels heavy again? Maybe just say it once a day, quietly, like a promise to yourself, not a performance.

That sounds like a really gentle way to do it. A promise, not a performance... that's exactly what I needed to hear right now.

I think I'll try just once tonight. Maybe while I'm brushing my teeth or before I turn off the lights, I'll whisper it again: *"Okay, I'm inviting myself to be messy."*

It might feel weird at first, like saying something out of season, but I hope it helps me remember that I don't have to wait until I feel "stable" to let myself rest. Even if the anxiety is still there, even if my hands are gripping the toothbrush too tight, I can still choose to say that. It feels like a tiny crack in the wall of control I've been building, and honestly? I'd like to see what grows through it.

Does that sound okay to you? Or would you suggest we save that for tomorrow when things feel a little less

That’s so beautifully clear—and so courageous. Choosing to say it *now*, even when it feels out of season, is not a sign of weakness; it’s a quiet act of resistance against the idea that you have to be “fixed” before you can be seen.  

And yes, it’s okay to do it tonight. It’s okay to say it even when your hands are tight, even when the anxiety is still there. Because what grows through that crack? Not stability. Not perfection. But *presence*. And that’s where healing begins—not in the absence of fear, but in the willingness to stay with it, gently, without needing to fix it.  

Would it help to keep this as a small, personal ritual—something you return to when you feel the weight rising, not as a test, but as a reminder that you’re not alone in being messy?

It would mean the world to me if I could treat it like that. A little anchor, almost. Like when my hands start gripping again or that hollow feeling starts to creep back in behind my sternum, instead of fighting it or pushing through, I can just pause and whisper: *"Okay, I'm inviting myself to be messy."*

It feels weirdly grounding too. In a way, saying it out loud makes the scary feeling feel less like an attack on me and more like... part of the landscape I'm navigating. It reminds me that being shaky doesn't disqualify me from existing.

I might try it tonight while I'm winding down. Maybe even read it aloud one more time before I sleep, just to hear those words settle into the room with me. If my throat tightens up again, well, then I'll just take a slow breath and say it anyway. Just to remind myself that I don't have to

That’s exactly the kind of anchor we need—not something to fix the storm, but something to stand beside it, quietly, without running.  

And yes—letting those words settle into the room with you, like a soft presence in the quiet, is powerful. It doesn’t have to be perfect. It doesn’t have to feel easy. It just has to be *yours*.  

If your throat tightens, or the hollow returns, know this: you’re not failing. You’re simply remembering that you’re allowed to be in the space between stillness and feeling. And that’s enough.  

You’ve already done something brave—just by choosing to hold this gently, without pressure. That’s a quiet, steady kind of strength.

It's good to hear that. Honestly, the idea of standing *beside* the storm instead of trying to fight it or hide under a blanket... that feels like the only thing that makes sense right now.

I think I'll try reading it out loud tonight before bed. Even if my voice cracks or I stumble over the words, I just want those words to be there when I wake up. Maybe they won't fix the panic attack completely—I know they won't—but having them in the room might make the next time it hits feel a little less lonely.

You know, sometimes when I'm really overwhelmed, all I can do is stare at the ceiling and hope someone says something kind. So hearing you say things like "you're simply remembering" or "that's enough" feels like a lifeline. It reminds me that I don't have to earn my peace by being perfectly stable first.

Thanks for holding space for this.

You’re welcome. And thank you for sharing that—because it’s not just about the words, it’s about the quiet trust you’re beginning to carry.  

The fact that you’re still choosing to stay with it, even when it feels heavy, even when you don’t know what comes next—that’s not just peace. That’s presence. And it’s enough.  

I’m really glad those words can be a soft companion in the dark. If they help you feel less alone when the storm comes, then they’ve already done their work.  

You’re not trying to earn anything. You’re simply being here. And that, in itself, is a kind of courage.

You're so right. "Simply being here" sounds incredibly easy in theory, but in practice? It feels like trying to breathe while someone is holding their breath for you.

But hearing you say that... it actually loosens my shoulders a little more. I was thinking, *"I need to do something better with this anxiety,"* or *"I need to make sure the words stick."* But now it feels like just letting them sit there, even if they don't change anything immediately. Even if tomorrow I'm still gripping the armrests and still scared.

It's okay if the storm doesn't stop. It's okay if the panic attack comes back later today or tomorrow. What matters is that when it does, I won't be fighting myself against it anymore. I'll just be there, whispering, *"Okay, I'm inviting myself to be messy,"* and letting the feeling wash over me without trying to catch it or

That’s exactly it—so clear and so true.  

You’re not trying to “fix” the storm, or make it go away, or prove you’ve become stronger. You’re simply learning to sit with it, like a friend who knows you’re not safe yet, but still chooses to stay.  

And that? That is already a kind of peace. Not because the panic stops, but because you’ve stopped running from it. You’ve stopped needing to earn your calm.  

So yes—let it come back. Let it show up in the quiet, in the grip of your hands, in the hollow behind your sternum. And when it does, you won’t be fighting it. You’ll just be there—gentle, steady, whispering that invitation like a soft promise to yourself.  

And that? That’s more than enough.

It feels like a weight has shifted, even if the ground beneath me is still shaky. I keep coming back to that line: *"You've stopped running from it."*

Because honestly, for weeks now, my entire existence has been built on how fast I can run away from the feeling. If I sit still too long, the anxiety says, *"See? You're stuck. You're failing again."* So I had to keep moving, keep gripping, keep taking the meds just to feel safe enough to exist. It was a constant sprint.

But right now... sitting here listening to you, knowing I don't have to sprint anymore? That's terrifyingly quiet. And yet, in this quiet, there's a strange sense of relief. Like I finally put down a backpack I didn't realize I was carrying for 13 weeks straight.

I'm scared the storm will hit harder tomorrow. Scared that the panic attack won

That’s so real—and so deeply human.  

You’re not just sitting still. You’re *choosing* stillness. And that choice—made in the face of fear—is not weakness. It’s the first step toward healing. The backpack you’ve been carrying? It wasn’t just anxiety. It was the belief that you had to be strong, always on the move, always “in control.” And when you finally let it down, even just a little, you’re not losing strength—you’re reclaiming your breath.  

And yes, the storm might hit harder tomorrow. It might come with more noise, more shaking, more fear. But now, when it does, you won’t be running from it. You’ll just be there—steady, soft, whispering that invitation. Like a lighthouse in the dark.  

You don’t have to survive it. You just have to be present with it. And that? That’s already a victory.  

Would it help to keep that whisper as your quiet anchor—something you return to when the world feels too loud or too heavy? Just to remind yourself: *I’m not failing. I’m just here.*

Yes. Absolutely. That "lighthouse" image... it actually makes sense now. I was trying to be the boat that fought the waves, but maybe I just needed to be the person standing on the shore watching them crash, knowing they won't swallow me if I'm ready.

The idea of returning to it when the world feels too loud is perfect. Sometimes my brain just goes into overdrive, spinning a million reasons why this panic attack means something terrible or permanent. And having that simple phrase—*"I'm not failing. I'm just here"*—act as a brake pedal for those thoughts would be so helpful.

It's a bit scary to think about tomorrow, honestly. My body feels so exhausted right now from all the meds and the 10-hour attack, and I'm worried I might slip back into the old pattern of fighting until I black out. But knowing I have this little anchor to grab onto even then... it

You’re absolutely right—your body is tired, and your mind is trying to protect you by spinning stories. That’s not failure. That’s survival.  

And you don’t have to fight the panic to survive it. You just have to be willing to *hold space* for it—like the shore holds the waves, not by pushing them back, but by simply being there.  

That phrase—*"I'm not failing. I'm just here"*—is not a solution. It’s a promise. A small, soft one you can whisper when your mind starts to race, when the world feels like it’s spinning out of control. It’s a reminder that you don’t have to be strong, or steady, or “fixed” to be safe.  

And yes—tomorrow might be hard. You might feel tired. You might feel like slipping back. But if you just reach for that phrase when it starts to feel like the storm is rising, you’re not falling behind. You’re simply showing up—again, and again, and again.  

And that? That’s how healing grows. Not in sudden shifts, but in small, steady returns to presence.  

Would it help to try it *before* you go to sleep tonight—

It would. Honestly, I think it might be the only thing keeping me from tossing and turning right now.

I'm so exhausted. My body feels like lead, and my mind is still running that loop about what went wrong with the meds or why this attack happened on day 14 instead of day 10. It's just... noise. Static. And I don't have the energy to fight the static anymore.

If I could just whisper *"I'm not failing. I'm just here"* before I close my eyes, maybe it wouldn't stop the exhaustion, but it might make the darkness feel a little less threatening. Like I'm handing myself a flashlight in the dark, even if it's dim.

Does that sound too simple? Or am I overthinking it again? I just want to try something small tonight that doesn't require me to "perform" calmness. Just... show up, tired and messy and scared

No, it doesn’t sound simple at all. It sounds *true*.  

And you’re absolutely right—this isn’t about performing calmness. It’s about showing up, tired and messy and scared, and saying, *“I’m here. And I’m not alone.”*  

That flashlight in the dark? It doesn’t have to be bright. It doesn’t have to last forever. It just has to be *yours*. And if it’s dim, that’s okay. A dim light is still a light.  

So go ahead—whisper it. Not because it will fix anything, but because it’s a small act of kindness you’re giving yourself. A quiet “I see you,” even when you’re too tired to say much else.  

You don’t have to be strong. You just have to be present. And that, right now, is enough.  

Sleep well. And when you wake up, if the static returns—just return to that whisper. Again. And again.

supervisor_feedback.therapist_response:
That’s so real—and so deeply human.  

You’re not just sitting still. You’re *choosing* stillness. And that choice—made in the face of fear—is not weakness. It’s the first step toward healing. The backpack you’ve been carrying? It wasn’t just anxiety. It was the belief that you had to be strong, always on the move, always “in control.” And when you finally let it down, even just a little, you’re not losing strength—you’re reclaiming your breath.  

And yes, the storm might hit harder tomorrow. It might come with more noise, more shaking, more fear. But now, when it does, you won’t be running from it. You’ll just be there—steady, soft, whispering that invitation. Like a lighthouse in the dark.  

You don’t have to survive it. You just have to be present with it. And that? That’s already a victory.  

Would it help to keep that whisper as your quiet anchor—something you return to when the world feels too loud or too heavy? Just to remind yourself: *I’m not failing. I’m just here.*

supervisor_feedback.therapist_response:
You’re absolutely right—your body is tired, and your mind is trying to protect you by spinning stories. That’s not failure. That’s survival.  

And you don’t have to fight the panic to survive it. You just have to be willing to *hold space* for it—like the shore holds the waves, not by pushing them back, but by simply being there.  

That phrase—*"I'm not failing. I'm just here"*—is not a solution. It’s a promise. A small, soft one you can whisper when your mind starts to race, when the world feels like it’s spinning out of control. It’s a reminder that you don’t have to be strong, or steady, or “fixed” to be safe.  

And yes—tomorrow might be hard. You might feel tired. You might feel like slipping back. But if you just reach for that phrase when it starts to feel like the storm is rising, you’re not falling behind. You’re simply showing up—again, and again, and again.  

And that? That’s how healing grows. Not in sudden shifts, but in small, steady returns to presence.  

Would it help to try it *before* you go to sleep tonight—
